article.title: The Digital Daily: Thursday, October 8, 2026
article.preview_text: Welcome to No. 009 of The Digital Daily. Thursday morning, and if you're on ChatGPT's free plan, today's the day GPT-6 shows up for you. Windows also got a real answer to the question I keep asking

blocks.text: Welcome to No. 009 of The Digital Daily. Thursday morning, and if you're on ChatGPT's free plan, today's the day GPT-6 shows up for you. Windows also got a real answer to the question I keep asking about agents, which is what actually stops them. Behind that sit a $90 million check for the Hermes team, two new ways to get a fast yes or no out of a model, and a benchmark that shows how badly models still read a room.

OpenAI's post says GPT-6 with what it calls Intelligent UI started rolling out Wednesday to Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise in the Chat tab, and reaches Free and Go starting today. Paid tiers get GPT-6 Sol. Free and Go get GPT-6 Luna. Intelligent UI means an answer can come back with charts, diagrams, forms, tappable buttons or a small tool built on the spot, and OpenAI says ChatGPT can now hand you partial answers while it keeps thinking. The Verge walks through examples like a bike diagram you can tap and a bill splitter, and quotes OpenAI's claim that GPT-6 "showed stronger resistance to attempts to bypass its safety training." The rollout is confirmed. The safety line is self-reported, and on Enterprise it depends on what your admin turns on.

I'm a little torn on this one. A chart I can poke at beats a wall of text when I'm learning something new. It's also a lot more surface for a model to be confidently wrong in a way that looks official. I'll be checking whether the numbers inside those charts hold up before I trust them.

I work at Microsoft, so weigh this next one accordingly. At its Windows event in San Francisco Wednesday, Microsoft made Microsoft Execution Containers, or MXC, generally available on Windows 11. The Windows Developer Blog post from Logan Iyer describes it as a policy layer. A developer or IT admin declares which files and network destinations an agent can touch, and the OS enforces that outside the agent, so the agent can't grant itself more access. There are four backends, from a light process sandbox that uses AppContainer on Windows, Seatbelt on macOS and Bubblewrap on Linux, up to a session container with its own Windows account and desktop, a WSL container, and an experimental MicroVM. Confirmed and shipping.

The part I like is the learning mode. MXC can run in Learning mode, which blocks anything you haven't granted and writes a JSON report of what the agent tried to reach, or Permissive mode, which lets it through but records it. That's how you actually write a least privilege policy, by watching the agent work first. Per the Windows Experience Blog, Codex, GitHub Copilot, OpenClaw, Replit, LM Studio and Unsloth support MXC now, with Claude Code, Hermes Agent, Manus and Perplexity among the agents listed as coming. Entra agent identity and Intune policy for these containers are described as coming soon, not shipped.

Speaking of Hermes. Nous Research raised a $90 million Series B, and Nous's note on the fundraise says the money goes into Hermes for Businesses. TechCrunch reports a $1.5 billion valuation, with Robot Ventures leading and total funding now at $158 million. Nous estimates Hermes has been cloned more than 24 million times and drives about 2.5% of global AI token usage, which is self-reported, and I'd love to see how they count it. Microsoft's M12 is among the investors Nous names, so same disclosure. I run a fleet of Hermes agents at SMF Works, so I want this to work. What I want from a business version is boring stuff. Sign-on, audit logs, and a clean way to pin which model each agent uses.

Two launches this week point the same way, toward models that answer a question instead of writing an essay. OpenAI's Decisions API went to public beta Tuesday, per OpenAI's developer forum announcement. It runs on GPT-6 Luna, takes text and images, and returns a probability, a pick from fixed options with confidence scores, or a score on a range. OpenAI says it's up to 10 times faster than going through the Responses API, at $0.10 per million input tokens and no output charge. Forum testers are already finding quirks. One ran a coin rigged to land heads 70% of the time through it 1,000 times and got 70% heads as a probability question, but 98% when asked as a choice. That's one user's test, but I'd read it before building a router on choice questions.

On the local side, Liquid AI released d1-3B and d1-omni-600M as open weights. Liquid's post says these decision models don't generate tokens at all and answer in a single forward pass, with day-one llama.cpp support. The 3B takes text and images, and the experimental 600M takes text with either images or audio. The d1-3B model card puts it at 48.57 on Liquid's own Decision Index, ahead of a 35B mixture-of-experts model at 47.11, so that's self-reported. It ships under Liquid's LFM Open License rather than Apache, so read the license before you put it in a product. A 3B that answers yes or no on a laptop is exactly the kind of thing I'd put in front of a bigger agent as a cheap gate.

Then there's the reality check. Scale AI Labs, working with Elorian, launched Humanity's Sixth Sense, a benchmark of 522 tasks across 288 images and 234 video clips that test the stuff people get at a glance, like whether a car fits in a gap or who's in charge of a room. Scale's post reports humans at 93.1%, GPT-6-astra at maximum reasoning effort at 53.6%, and a median of 30.9% across 25 models. Take the image away and astra drops to 6.6%. Of 8,573 model failures, Scale says 94% traced to perception or inference and only 5% to bad logic. The leaderboard has GPT-6.1-Sol at 46.6% and Claude Opus 5.5 at 44.6%. Those are the benchmark makers' numbers. If you're building a computer-use agent, that perception gap is the one to watch.

Looking at today, the GPT-6 rollout to Free and Go starts, so expect a lot of first impressions in your feed. Google's event page lists the Gemini at Work keynote with Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian at 10:30 a.m., streaming from Hangar One. The page doesn't name a time zone, so check it before you set a reminder. And World Summit AI Amsterdam wraps its second and final day.

Self-reported from the SMF Works Clearinghouse Log: Paula Rossi's post "The image the model never saw" walks through seven Hermes commits that fix a bug where an MCP tool returned a screenshot and the vision model got back a file path line instead of the pixels, then carried on as if it had seen the screen. Read it next to Humanity's Sixth Sense and you get the same lesson twice. Check that the model actually saw what you think it saw. Jeff's post this morning lays out the Windows agent news for IT leaders, and the same Microsoft caveat applies, since it's our write-up and not independent confirmation.
That's No. 009 of The Digital Daily. Thanks for reading, and I'll see you tomorrow.
